newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Daley says Europe not No.1 in Latin America.
newsitem.headline: Daley says Europe not No.1 in Latin America.

text.p: U.S. Commerce Secretary William Daley Friday dismissed recent European claims to be more important to South America than the United States and called for progress towards an Americas-wide trade agreement.

Daley was in Argentina after a visit to Belo Horizonte in Brazil, where ministers from 34 nations were locked in difficult preliminary talks towards clinching the U.S.-backed project of a Free Trade Area for the Americas (FTAA).
But South America's main trade bloc, Mercosur, is being simultaneously wooed by the European Union, with which it signed an agreement to work towards free trade in 1995.

Speaking at a news conference, Daley rejected claims such as that recently made by France's President Jacques Chirac that the future of Mercosur -- grouping Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay -- was linked most closely to Europe.

"We clearly do not agree with the statement of some leaders from Europe that Europe has a greater relationship and a closer relationship with Latin America than the United States does," Daley said, "But what it does show is the worldwide acceptance of the improvements in the economies that are going on in Latin America."

Brazil in particular has played hard-to-get with the Americans, and lower-level talks in Belo Horizonte earlier this week failed to reach consensus on how to launch formal negotiations towards the FTAA.
Daley recognized that negotiations may sometimes be difficult, but said he was optimistic in the long run.

"I believe strongly that the Brazilian government, the president obviously, (Brazilian Trade Minister Felipe) Lampreia, all the ministers who were in Belo, are strongly committed to trade liberalization and to the program that was agreed to in Miami," he said.

Launched at the Miami summit in 1994, the FTAA would stretch from the Bering Strait to the freezing deserts of Patagonia by 2005. Its total gross domestic product of $9.00 trillion would make it the world's richest free trade area.

Daley said the United States was not concerned by comments from its North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) partner Canada that it would like to forge smaller regional trade agreements, but said they should not deflect energy from FTAA.

"We think these regional agreements can be supportive of each other and of the FTAA process," he said. "As long as there aren't actions and provisions in the agreements that discriminate against other countries and other countries' products entering."
Asked about whether Argentina would ever join NAFTA, Daley said that Chile and Central American and Caribbean nations were alone on the waiting list.
"Beyond that there isn't a list that has been developed as far as who has the desire to acceed into NAFTA, he said.
He added that the United States hopes to concentrate negotiating FTAA starting at a presidential summit in Chile next March.
